parole.significato: A suffix forming infinitives of fourth conjugation verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -īre, the ending of the present active infinitive form of fourth conjugation verbs. Cognate with Spanish and French -ir, Italian -ire, etc.
Inherited from Latin -tātem, accusative of -tās, from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts.
Inherited from Latin -am, from Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂.
From Latin ad, from Proto-Indo-European *ád (“near; at”).
Inherited from Latin acus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”).
Inherited from Latin adiungō (“add, join to”), from ad + iungō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yewg-.
Inherited from Latin amārus (“bitter”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₃- (“to be hot”).
Inherited from Latin aqua, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂. Compare Aromanian apã, Megleno-Romanian apu, Istro-Romanian åpę and Sardinian abba.
Inherited from Latin arcus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷo-.
Inherited from Latin aries, arietem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁r-i-(e)t- (“certain domestic animal”).

parole.significato: an animal's haunch, or a thigh on a person
parole.testo: From Latin armus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to join”).
Inherited from Latin asperum, singular accusative of asper (“rough”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂esp- (“to cut”).

Inherited from Latin sūdāre, from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-. The prefix is a later innovation carrying no semantic nor grammatical nuance, typically seen in Aromanian and less so but still occasionally in Romanian and it's regional varieties.

parole.significato: to hear (to perceive with the ear)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin audīre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-is-d-, a compound of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from the root *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”)) and *dʰh₁-ye/o- (“to render”).

Probably from Latin avus, normally resulting in *au, with a diminutive suffix -uș added. Was once found in the Oltenia region but has disappeared from spoken language. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwh₂os (“grandfather”). Already present in Appendix Probi (avus non aus). Compare Aromanian a
Inherited from Latin acia, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”).
Inherited from Latin carpinus, probably from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂er- (“hard”).
Inherited from Latin quid, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís.
Inherited from Latin cervus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂wós, from *ḱerh₂- (“horn”). Compare Aromanian tserbu.
Inherited from Latin cervīcem, accusative of cervīx, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head”) and *weyk- (“to bend”). Doublet of the borrowed cervix.
Inherited from Latin clāmāre, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to shout”). Compare Aromanian cljem, cljimari, Italian chiamare, Neapolitan chiammà. Doublet of clama, which was borrowed from French.

Inherited from Latin clārus, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”). Doublet of clar, which was a borrowing. Used almost always as an adverb in modern speech (compare Latin pure, adverb form of purus). The old adjective form is only found in old texts and in some expressions such as "di
Inherited from Latin corvus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂wós. Compare Aromanian corbu, Albanian korb, Italian corvo.

parole.significato: crust (outside layer formed by solidifying, drying etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin crusta (possibly a later borrowing; cf. French croûte, German Kruste), from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”).
Inherited from Latin crepāre, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂-.
Inherited from Latin cuneus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱū (“sting”).
Inherited from Latin quod, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. Compare Aromanian cã, che.
Inherited from Latin carbōnem, accusative of carbō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ker (“to burn”). Doublet of carbon, a borrowing from French.
Inherited from Latin damnum, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂pnom (“expense, investment”).
Inherited from Latin digitus, from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”). Compare Aromanian dzeadzit. Doublet of digit.
Inherited from Latin dēnsus (“dense; frequent”), from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”). Doublet of dens, a borrowing.
Inherited from Latin dis-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís.

Inherited from Latin dentem, the singular accusative of dēns, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts. Compare Spanish diente, Catalan dent, French dent, Italian dente and Aromanian dinti.
Inherited from Latin favus, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōw- (“to swell, grow, thrive, be, live, dwell”).

parole.significato: old unit of measurement (used in Moldova) in agriculture equivalent to about half a hectare, or an area of land that si…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin falx, falcem (“sickle”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelk-, *dʰelg- (“a cutting tool”). Cf. Medieval Latin falcata. See also the related form falcă (“jaw”), which underwent further semantic evolution from the original etymology of "sickle" in Latin.

Probably from Latin ferīre (“strike”), of Proto-Indo-European origin, with a related but shifted semantic development in Romanian (with the meaning seeming to derive from the reaction to being struck or attacked). Other less likely explanations include a Vulgar Latin *auferīre, from an alteration of
Inherited from Latin fēlīx, fēlīcem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-lw-i, from *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle”).
Inherited from Latin fera, from ferus (“wild animal”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwer-.
Inherited from Latin fīlum, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰiH-(s-)lo-.
Inherited from Latin follis, follem, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolǵʰnis, derivative of *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”).

Inherited from Latin famēs, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Galician fame, French faim, Italian fame and Portuguese fome. The Romanian phonetic development was unusual in this case, with the diphthong -oa- normally resulting from a Latin -o-; however, compare the aforementio

From the Latin adjective fortis, fortem, from Old Latin forctis, fortis, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise, high, hill”). Compare the same semantic development in French fort, Occitan fòrça, Ligurian foart (attested in Menton, France). In older Romanian, the word was also used as a freesta
Inherited from Latin fraxinus, from *bʰr̥Hǵ-s-inos, adjective of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵos (“birch”). Compare Aromanian frapsin.
Inherited from Latin frīgus (“cold”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sriHgos-, *sriges-, *sriHges-.
Inherited from Latin frīgere, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.
Inherited from Latin frontem f (“forehead”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰron-t-, from *bʰren- (“project”).
Inherited from Latin frangere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-.

Inherited from Latin fūlīginem, accusative singular of fūlīgo, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂li-, from *dʰewh₂-. The expected Romanian result would have been *furigine, but was probably modified through assimilation or a hypercorrection to rhotacism.
Inherited from Latin formīca or furmīca, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *morwi-. Compare Aragonese fornica, Aromanian furnicã.

parole.significato: to fuck (to engage in sexual intercourse, crudely)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin futuere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to hit”). Compare Aromanian fut.
Inherited from Latin fēnum, from faenum, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-, from *dʰeh₁(y)-.
Inherited from Latin fētus (“offspring, progreny”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-. Doublet of fetus.

parole.significato: frost (cold weather that causes frost to form)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin gelū, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).

Inherited from Latin glomus, probably through a Vulgar Latin *glemus. Or altered within Romanian from *ghiom > *ghiome (plural form) to *gheme and finally analogically back a singular. Compare Aromanian gljem, gljom. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“form into a ball; ball”).

Inherited from Latin glāns, glāndem, probably through the now archaic, dialectal form ghinde or through an intermediate Vulgar Latin root *glanda with change in declension. Compare Aromanian gljindã, Italian ghianda. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂- (“acorn”).
Inherited from Latin gener, generi, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵm̥ros, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-.
Inherited from Latin gingīva, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-. Compare Aromanian dzindzii, dzindzie.
Inherited from Latin grandinem, accusative singular of grandō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₃d-.
Inherited from Latin gruem, accusative of grūs /gruis (“crane”), from Proto-Indo-European *gr̥h₂ú-, from *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”).
Inherited from Latin grumus, from Proto-Indo-European *gar-, *ger- (“to tie, bind together”).
Inherited from Latin volvere (“turn, tumble”), with a change in conjugation; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welw-, *wel- (“to turn, wind, round”). Compare Aromanian nvolbu, nvulbari, volbu.
Inherited from Latin equa, feminine form of equus (“horse”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éḱwos (“horse”).
Inherited from Latin herba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”). Compare Aromanian earbã.
Inherited from Latin hedera, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to seize, grasp, take”).
Inherited from Latin līmus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyH- (“to smear”).
Inherited from Latin ānellus, diminutive of ānus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₂no- (“ring”).
Inherited from Latin juvencus, iuvencus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁n̥ḱós, derived from *h₂yuh₁en-, derived from the root *h₂ey- (“vital force”, “life”).
From Latin lavāre, from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash”). The form la developed from an older lăa, which itself is from an older lăua. The Transylvanian variant lăia is derived from one.

Inherited from Latin lacus (“lake”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”). Compare Aragonese laco, Catalan llac, Esperanto lago, French lac, Italian lago, Maltese lag, Portuguese lago, Sardinian lagu, Spanish lago.
From the older form lacrămă, from Latin lacrima, from Old Latin lacruma, dacrima, dacruma, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru-.
Inherited from Latin lātus (“wide”), from earlier stlātus, from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to stretch out, extend, spread”) or *stelh₃- (“broad”).
Deverbal from lăuda or inherited from Latin laudem, accusative of laus, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lēwt-, *lēwdʰ- (“song, sound”), from *lēw- (“to sound, resound, sing out”).
Inherited from Latin ligāre, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).
Inherited from Latin lignum, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-no- (“that which is collected”), from *leǵ-. Compare Aromanian lemnu or lem.
From the Latin longus (“long”, adjective), from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós (“long”).
Inherited from Latin lunter, luntrem, variant of linter (“small boat, skiff”). Cf. Ancient Greek πλυντήρ (pluntḗr). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plew- (“to wash”).

parole.significato: lean, meager, without fat or low-fat
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin macrum, accusative singular of macer, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós.
Inherited from Latin marginem, accusative of margō (“edge, margin”), from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs.
Inherited from Latin milium, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).

Inherited from Latin mergere, itself ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mesg- (“to plunge, dip”), with a unique sense developing in Balkanic or Eastern Romance. Compare Aromanian njergu; cf. also Albanian mërgoj (“to move away”) and Sardinian imbergere (“to push”). The semantic shift could be owed
Inherited from Latin mollis, mollem, from earlier *molduis, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dus (“soft, weak”), from *mel- (“soft, weak, tender”). Compare Aromanian moali.
Inherited from Latin mors, from Proto-Indo-European *mértis (“death”), from *mer- (“to die”).
Inherited from Latin mola, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).
Inherited from Latin mūgīre, from Proto-Indo-European *mug-, *mūg-, of onomatopoetic origin.
Inherited from Latin multus, from the Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle).
Inherited from Latin montem, accusative of mōns, from Proto-Indo-European *men-. Compare Aromanian munti.
Inherited from Latin musca, from Proto-Indo-European *mus- (“a fly”).

parole.significato: unfermented wine; grape or other fruit juice
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mustum, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-, *mews- (“damp”).
Inherited from Latin mūtus, of Proto-Indo-European origin.
Inherited from Latin māne, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, mature”). Compare Aromanian mãni.

parole.significato: to spend the night, take shelter (for the night), put up
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin manēre, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stay, stand still”).
Inherited from Latin me (accusative singular of ego), from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)me.
Inherited from Latin nāvis, nāvem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Compare the borrowed doublet navă.
Inherited from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.

parole.significato: fog (cloud that forms at a low altitude and obscures vision)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin nebula, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud”). Compare Aromanian negurã.
Inherited from Latin ningere (“to snow”), present infinitive of ningit, ningo, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sneygʷʰ- (“to snow”).
Inherited from Latin nōdus, from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”).

From older nuar, nuăr, from Latin nūbilum, noun use of the neuter of the adjective nūbilus (“cloudy”), from Latin nūbēs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)newdʰ- (“to cover”). Compare Aromanian nior, Spanish nube, Italian nuvola, Friulian nûl, Portuguese nuvem, Catalan núvol, Provençal nyiuro,
Inherited from Latin novem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.
Inherited from Latin nōmen, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥. The presence of the -u- may indicate some influence from număr.
Inherited from Latin numerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”).
Inherited from Latin octō, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.
Inherited from Latin orbus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”). Compare Italian orbo. Doublet of rob.
Inherited from Latin hordeum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥sdeyom (“bristly”).
Inherited from Latin pācem, accusative of pāx (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-.

parole.significato: palm (the inner concave of the hand)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin palma, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂. Compare Aromanian palmã.
Inherited from Latin passer, passerem (“sparrow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *p(e)t-tro- (“who flies, bird”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”).
Inherited from Latin piscem, apparently a blend of the singular and plural forms. ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-. Cognates include Italian pesce, Spanish pez, peje and Portuguese peixe.
Inherited from Latin pellis, pellem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).

Inherited from Latin pēdem, accusative of pēs, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds. The original sense of "foot" was attested in 17th century texts, but it later came to be used in a mostly figurative sense as it underwent semantic evolution. The development of this figurative sense (from which other exp
Inherited from Latin pīnus, ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *poi- (“sap, juice”).

Inherited from Latin plicāre (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”). Compare Aromanian plec, plicari. The semantic shift from "fold" to "leave" may be because to Proto-Romanian speakers, the word became associated with the folding up of tents to leave and move, especiall
Inherited from Latin porta (“door, gate”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to pass through”).

Inherited from Latin palumbus (“wood-pigeon, ringdove”), palumbes, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pal-wo (“dark-colored, gray”). The sense of "maize" or "corn" developed probably due to the similarity in appearance of a corn cob to the bird (a similar development occurred in Bulgarian or was c
Inherited from Latin praeda, from earlier praeheda, from prae + Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.
Inherited from Latin pretium, from Proto-Indo-European *préti (“back”).
Inherited from Latin prēndere, alternative form of prehendere, from prae- (“before”) + *hendō (“to take, seize”) (not attested without prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.
Inherited from Latin prandium, of Proto-Indo-European origin. Compare Italian pranzo, Aromanian prãndzu.
Inherited from Latin pulverem, accusative of pulvis, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”). Doublet of pudră, taken from French.
Inherited from Latin pulpa, from Old Latin *pelpa, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”).
Inherited from Latin pūlicem, singular accusative of pūlex, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plus-.
Inherited from Latin portāre (“to carry, bring”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“go, traverse”). Compare Neapolitan purtà.

parole.significato: well (both for water and oil, gas, etc)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin puteus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *paw- (“to strike”).
Inherited from Latin pānis, pānem, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to feed, to graze”). Compare Aromanian pãni.
Inherited from Latin pilus, from Proto-Indo-European *pil-.
Inherited from Latin rāmus, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”).
Inherited from Latin rōdere, from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₃d- (“to gnaw, scrape, scratch”).
Inherited from Latin rota, from Proto-Indo-European *Hret- (“to roll”).

Inherited from Latin rōs, rōrem, possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *rovem through analogy with other words like bos, whence bovem. Another theory suggests an initial early Romanian form *roor, resulting in a plural *rouri which was reformed into a singular analogically. Compare also the change of

parole.significato: to ask politely, to say please
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin rogāre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵ-, ablaut of *h₃reǵ-.
Inherited from Latin salix, from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥H-ik- (“willow”).
Inherited from Latin sarcina (“pack, burden”), from Proto-Indo-European *serk- (“to fence”).
Inherited from Latin scūtum (“shield”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skei- (“to cut, split”), an extension of *sek- (“to cut”). Doublet of escudo.
Inherited from Latin siccus, from Proto-Indo-European *seyk-.
Inherited from Latin secāre, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).
Inherited from Latin signum, of Proto-Indo-European origin.
Inherited from Latin servāre, from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to watch over, protect”).
Inherited from Latin sitis, sitem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰítis (“perishing, decrease”).
Inherited from Latin sēbum, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out”).

parole.significato: to feel (of both tangibles and intangibles)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sentīre, from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”).
Inherited from Latin sōl, sōlem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥.
Inherited from Latin somnus, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
Inherited from Latin socius (“partner”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-yo- (“companion”), from *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Compare Aromanian sots.
Inherited from Latin spargere (“scatter”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pregʰ- (“to scatter, to jerk”).

parole.significato: the space between a roller or cylinder and the comb on a weaving loom; the part of the fabric not yet rolled on the rol…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin spatium, from Proto-Indo-European *speh₁- (“to stretch, to pull”). Compare spațiu (a borrowed doublet), with a more general sense.
Inherited from Latin super, from *eks-uper, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs (“out of”) (Latin ex) and *uperi (“above”), from *upo. Doublet of super.
Inherited from Latin stāre, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-.
Inherited from Latin stringere (“tighten”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *streyg-.

parole.significato: thrush (any of several species of songbirds of the family Turdidae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin turdus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos. The initial s- may be due to influence by Latin sturnus, and the final -z may be due to the word being reformed from the plural *turzi, or less likely through a Vulgar Latin root *turdeus. Compare Aromanian sturdzu, strudz.
Inherited from Latin sūgere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sug-, *suk-.

parole.significato: furrow of earth (alternating with a ditch or pit)
parole.testo: Probably from Latin sulcus, corresponding to Proto-Indo-European *solk-o- (“furrow”), *selk- (“to pull, drag”).

parole.significato: to ring or produce a sound in general
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sonāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”). First attested in 1581.
Inherited from Latin surdus, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“ringing, whistling”). Compare Aromanian surdu.
Inherited from Latin salīre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥-ye-. Cognate with Italian salire (“to go up”).

Inherited from Latin tata, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tatás. Compare Aromanian tatã, Dalmatian tuota (“father”), Neapolitan tata (“father”); cf. also Albanian tatë. It was possibly reinforced by the similar South Slavic term (e.g. Serbo-Croatian tata (“dad”)).
Inherited from Latin taurus, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros.
From Latin tē (accusative of tū), from Proto-Indo-European *twé, *te, accusative of *túh₂ (“you”).
Inherited from Latin tempus (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”), from the root *temp- (“to stetch, string”).
Inherited from Latin tonāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”).
Inherited from Latin tussis, tussem, from Proto-Indo-European *tud-ti-s- (“cough”), from *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”).
Inherited from Latin ulmus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”).
Inherited from Latin umbra (“shadow”), probably from Old Latin *omra, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂mr-u-, *h₂mrup-. Compare Aromanian aumbrã.
Inherited from Latin humerus, from umerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃émsos (“shoulder”).
Inherited from Latin ululāre, through Vulgar Latin ūrulāre, ultimately from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root.
Inherited from Latin ornus, influenced by ulm. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃s-.
Inherited from Latin virga, probably from Proto-Indo-European *wisgā (“flexible rod or stick”).
Borrowed from French vice- and Latin vice-.
Inherited from Latin venter, ventrem, from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri-.
Borrowed from Latin vōx, vōcem, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs. Compare French voix, Italian voce, Spanish voz. Replaced the older inherited form boace (a doublet).

parole.significato: vein, or blood vessel in general
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vēna, of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin. Doublet of venă, a borrowing.

Inherited from Latin (cōnsobrīnus) vērus (“true cousin”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros, from *weh₁- (“true”). Cf. Aromanian ver and cusurin. For the semantic evolution compare Spanish and Portuguese primo.
Inherited from Latin decem, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.
Inherited from Latin angustus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enǵʰu-, from *h₂enǵʰ-.
Inherited from Latin inter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”).
Inherited from Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
Inherited from Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

Probably from Latin termen, an older alternative form of terminus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through”). The archaic variant form țărmur(e) may have been the original, from which the modern form developed analogically, re-interpreted as a singular from the plural țărmuri. To explain
